meta.title: Can Trust in Science Be Improved? An Adaptive Experiment Testing Student-Designed Messages

exploratory.title: Planned H1 estimates restricted to finished responses
exploratory.rationale: Unfinished responses make up a sizeable share of the sample, so the planned arm contrasts are re-estimated on completed surveys to check that the registered pattern does not depend on partial responses.
exploratory.method: The planned treatment-versus-control comparisons on trust in science were re-estimated with the same specification on the subset of respondents who finished the survey, and the arm estimates and standard errors were set side by side with the original ones.
exploratory.finding: The finished-only sample is the same 7,803 respondents as the main model (every analysed respondent finished the survey), so all 32 arm estimates and standard errors are identical, with 5 arms significant at p<0.05 in both. The check cannot test sensitivity to partial completion.

exploratory.title: Heterogeneity of planned H1 arm effects by Republican identification
exploratory.rationale: Partisanship is the most likely source of variation in trust in science, so the planned arm contrasts are checked for differences between Republicans and non-Republicans.
exploratory.method: The planned treatment-versus-control comparisons were re-estimated with an interaction between each arm and a 0/1 indicator of Republican identification, and the interaction estimates were tabulated.
exploratory.finding: One of 32 arm-by-Republican interactions is significant at p<0.05: the everyday-science student video (Science in everyday life) raised trust about 0.17 points more among Republicans (p = 0.004). Three text messages have interactions with p between 0.05 and 0.08. With 32 uncorrected tests, this is a lead for follow-up, not evidence of partisan heterogeneity overall.

lit.text: The retrieved literature on the hypothesis is thin. Van Bavel et al. (2020) argue that social and behavioural science should inform the COVID-19 pandemic response, which gives general backing to testing whether brief messages can shape public attitudes toward science. Ecker et al. (2022) review the psychological drivers of misinformation belief and its resistance to correction, which bears on whether any single message can move trust in science relative to a pure control. Berinsky et al. (2012) assess the internal and external validity of experiments run on Amazon Mechanical Turk, a relevant reference for an online randomised design. The main tension is between the expectation that messages can shift trust and Ecker et al.'s account of how resistant beliefs are to correction. Van Bavel et al. take the policy case for behavioural interventions as given, while Ecker et al. suggest that changing entrenched beliefs is hard. A design with 32 messages against a pure control can test whether any message departs from control, which speaks directly to this disagreement. Berinsky et al.'s validity concerns mean that any such effects would need to be read with the sample's limits in mind.

sections.abstract: Can brief, student-designed messages raise trust in science? We ran a registered online survey experiment with US adults recruited through Lucid, randomly assigning respondents to one of 32 messages (videos, texts, memes, posters and infographics) or a pure control that only asked them to continue. Of 11,519 raw responses, 8,572 were analysed. Trust in science was measured after treatment on a scale where the control mean was 3.685. One video, 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?', lowered trust by 0.171 points (95% CI [−0.262, −0.080], p < 0.001), and the 'Powers of Ten' clip lowered it by 0.104 points. Three videos raised trust by roughly 0.06 points each: the peer-review video and two student-made videos. For the other arms the results were inconclusive; their intervals were wide and do not rule out small effects. Tests were uncorrected for multiplicity and several arms were small, so the modest findings should be read cautiously.
sections.design_notes: The plan was registered on OSF, with later amendments covering the assignment algorithm and covariate adjustment. The sample is US adults from Lucid. There were 11,519 raw responses and 8,572 in the analysis; the model for H1 used 7,803 rows with complete data. Arms were assigned adaptively, so arm sizes vary widely, from about 116 to 921 respondents. Each message is compared with the pure control. The outcome is trust in science measured after treatment, with a control mean of 3.685.

results.H1: Five of the 32 messages had uncorrected two-sided p < 0.05. The 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video lowered trust by 0.171 points (95% CI [−0.262, −0.080], p < 0.001), and the 'Powers of Ten' clip by 0.104 points (95% CI [−0.184, −0.024], p = 0.010). Three videos raised it by about 0.06 points: Science through the day (95% CI [0.016, 0.111], p = 0.009), Science in everyday life (95% CI [0.014, 0.112], p = 0.012) and the peer-review video (95% CI [0.005, 0.123], p = 0.034). The remaining arms had intervals including zero, so they are inconclusive rather than shown to be ineffective. With 32 uncorrected tests, the p-values near 0.03 deserve particular caution.

exploratory.E1: Exploratory, unreviewed code: the finished-only subset equals the analysed sample (7,803 rows in both), so the check is uninformative about whether incomplete responses matter.
exploratory.E2: Exploratory, unreviewed code: one arm-by-Republican-identification interaction was significant at p < 0.05, and the others were imprecise. Partisan differences are therefore not established.

sections.limitations: Thirty-two two-sided tests were run without correction for multiplicity, so some of the five effects with p < 0.05 may be false positives, especially those with p near 0.03. Adaptive assignment left some arms with only about 120 respondents, giving wide intervals. The effects are small, at most about 0.17 points on the trust scale, and only trust measured right after exposure is observed, so durability is unknown. Lucid is an online panel, so results may not generalise beyond it. Several messages differ in format, length and content, so the design cannot say which feature drives an effect.

extensions.title: Replicating the short student videos with a delayed follow-up and a behavioural outcome
extensions.why: Addresses power and measurement. It concentrates the sample on the two best-supported arms plus the peer-review video, tests them against control in a confirmatory design, and adds a delayed and a behavioural outcome.

power_target.basis: Observed effect of about 0.063 (SE 0.025 at n=853-921). The power table was empty, so the sample size is a back-of-envelope estimate of about 1,000 per arm for 80% power at 0.063. 4,000 per arm gives headroom to detect effects of about half that size and for attrition in the delayed wave.

extensions.rationale: In the source study, Science through the day (about 0.06, SE 0.025) and Science in everyday life (0.063, SE 0.025) were near the threshold among 32 uncorrected tests. The peer-review video had 0.064 (p=0.034). Only immediate trust was measured, so durability and behavioural carry-over are unknown. This confirmatory test concentrates the sample on those three videos plus control and adds a 7-day and a behavioural outcome.
extensions.contribution: Provides a Holm-corrected confirmatory test of whether short science videos raise trust, whether any effect lasts 7 days, and whether it changes a behavioural choice.
extensions.hypothesis: Each video raises immediate trust relative to control (position a). Under position b, contrasts are near zero after Holm correction. Effects at 7 days are smaller than or equal to immediate effects.
extensions.primary_outcome: Immediate post-treatment trust in science (mean of 6 items, items 4-6 reverse-coded), with 7-day trust and the behavioural choice as secondary outcomes.
extensions.comparison: Each of the three videos against control, with Holm correction across the three contrasts, covariate-adjusted for pre-treatment trust.

extensions.why: Addresses design confounding. It tests whether the small gains reflect content or merely an attention cue, which discriminates between the brief-messages-work and beliefs-resist positions.

extensions.rationale: In the source study, the 29-second student video 'Science in everyday life' raised trust by 0.063 (SE 0.025, p=0.012), but it differs from other arms in format, length and content, and 32 uncorrected tests were run. A 2x2 of content by format with a pure control tests whether such small gains come from the science framing or from an attention cue.
extensions.contribution: Separates content from format and salience in a brief trust-in-science message, which discriminates between the brief-messages-work and beliefs-resist positions.
extensions.hypothesis: If content drives the effect (position a), only the two science-framing cells raise trust relative to control and neutral cells. If salience or format alone drives it, neutral cells also move trust. If beliefs resist (position b), all contrasts are near zero.

We ran a registered online survey experiment with US adults recruited through Lucid, randomly assigning respondents to one of 32 messages (videos, texts, memes, posters and infographics) or a pure control that only asked them to continue. Of 11,519 raw responses, 8,572 were analysed. Trust in science was measured after treatment on a scale where the control mean was 3.685. One video, 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?', lowered trust by 0.171 points (95% CI [−0.262, −0.080], p < 0.001), and the 'Powers of Ten' clip lowered it by 0.104 points. Three videos raised trust by roughly 0.06 points each: the peer-review video and two student-made videos. The other arms were not distinguishable from control. Effects are small, tests were uncorrected for multiplicity, and several arms were small, so the modest findings should be read cautiously.
sections_draft.design_notes: The plan was registered on OSF, with later amendments covering the assignment algorithm and covariate adjustment. The sample is US adults from Lucid. There were 11,519 raw responses and 8,572 in the analysis; the model for H1 used 7,803 rows with complete data. Arms were assigned adaptively, so arm sizes vary widely, from about 116 to 921 respondents. Each message is compared with the pure control. The outcome is trust in science measured after treatment, with a control mean of 3.685.

results.H1: Five of the 32 messages differed from control, using two-sided p-values. The 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video lowered trust by 0.171 points (95% CI [−0.262, −0.080], p < 0.001), and the 'Powers of Ten' clip by 0.104 points (95% CI [−0.184, −0.024], p = 0.010). Three videos raised it by about 0.06 points: Science through the day (95% CI [0.016, 0.111], p = 0.009), Science in everyday life (95% CI [0.014, 0.112], p = 0.012) and the peer-review video (95% CI [0.005, 0.123], p = 0.034). The remaining arms had intervals including zero, so they are inconclusive rather than shown to be ineffective. With 32 uncorrected tests, the p-values near 0.03 deserve particular caution.

exploratory.E1: Exploratory, unreviewed code: restricting to finished responses gave estimates essentially identical to the original ones, with the same five arms at p < 0.05. This agrees with the registered estimates.
exploratory.E2: Exploratory, unreviewed code: only 1 of 32 arm-by-Republican-identification interactions had p < 0.05, about what chance would produce. This gives no clear sign of partisan differences, though the check is imprecise.

sections_draft.limitations: Thirty-two two-sided tests were run without correction for multiplicity, so some of the five significant effects may be false positives, especially those with p near 0.03. Adaptive assignment left some arms with only about 120 respondents, giving wide intervals. The effects are small, at most about 0.17 points on the trust scale, and only trust measured right after exposure is observed, so durability is unknown. Lucid is an online panel, so results may not generalise beyond it. Several messages differ from each other in format, length and content, so the design cannot say which feature drives an effect.

got_right: Pre-registered design with documented amendments (assignment algorithm, Lin covariate adjustment) and a pure control, so each of the 32 messages is a clean randomized contrast.
Broad stimulus set (videos, text, memes, posters, infographics), including student-made messages, with a pre-treatment trust covariate that tightens intervals (SEs of about 0.025-0.046).
Honest reporting: non-significant arms are called inconclusive, and the multiplicity and small-arm caveats are stated.

The student-made videos 'Science through the day' (n=921) and 'Science in everyday life' (n=853) were the best-powered arms and gave consistent estimates (0.063 each), so they are the most credible positive result.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Adaptive assignment left most arms at about 116-180 respondents against a control of 664. Intervals are too wide to rule out effects of 0.1 for most arms, and the positive effects are close to the noise floor.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: Arm n of 116-180 with SEs of 0.035-0.056. The control has n=664, and the peer-review video has p=0.034.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Thirty-two uncorrected two-sided tests were run, and 5 reached p<0.05, roughly the 1.6 expected by chance. Only the 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video (p=0.0002) clearly survives a Bonferroni threshold of about 0.0016.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: H1 table: p=0.034, 0.012, 0.009 and 0.010 for the other four significant arms.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Trust is a single post-treatment measure with a ceiling-like control mean of 3.685. Effects of about 0.06 are tiny, and durability is unknown.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: Control mean 3.685. Largest effect -0.171. The Limitations section says only immediate trust is observed.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: The arms vary in format, length and content at once, so no active ingredient can be identified. The positive student videos are also short and generic.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: Student videos last about 29 s. The negative arms are a limits-of-science video and a 'Powers of Ten' clip.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: The exploratory partisan check suggests heterogeneity in at least one arm, but the study was not powered to test it.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: E2: the Science in everyday life interaction with Republican identification is 0.165 (p=0.004). Climate skeptic converts is 0.178 (p=0.053). 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' is 0.191 (p=0.173).

debates.label: Can brief messages move trust in science?
debates.position_a: Brief, well-designed messages and behavioural interventions can shift public attitudes toward science.
debates.position_b: Entrenched beliefs resist correction, so single brief messages leave trust largely unchanged relative to control.
debates.what_this_study_says: The evidence leans toward position b. Most of the 32 messages are inconclusive, and the significant effects are at most 0.06 points up and 0.17 down. Small positive shifts from short student videos cannot be ruled out, but they are not robust to multiplicity.

briefs.title: Replicating the short student videos with a delayed follow-up and a behavioural outcome
briefs.question: Do short everyday-science student videos raise trust in science, and does the effect persist a week later and carry over to a behavioural choice?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Addresses power and measurement. It concentrates the sample on the two best-supported arms plus the peer-review video, tests them against control in a confirmatory design, and adds a delayed and a behavioural outcome.
briefs.design_sketch: Four arms: Science through the day, Science in everyday life, the peer-review video, and a pure control. Fixed equal allocation, with pre-treatment trust measured. Outcomes are immediate trust, trust at 7 days, and a behavioural choice (such as donating a bonus to a science organisation or choosing a science-based news article). Analysis is registered, with Holm correction across the three treatment contrasts.

power_target.basis: Observed effect of about 0.063 (SE 0.025 at n=853-921). The power table was empty, so the sample size is a back-of-envelope estimate of about 1,000 per arm for 80% power at 0.063. 4,000 per arm gives headroom to detect effects of about half that size and for attrition in the delayed wave.

briefs.title: Format versus content: separating persuasion from salience
briefs.question: Do short messages shift trust through their content or through format and salience alone?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Addresses design confounding. It tests whether the small gains reflect content or merely an attention cue, which discriminates between the brief-messages-work and beliefs-resist positions.
briefs.design_sketch: A 2x2 factorial. One factor is content (everyday-science framing versus neutral content of the same length). The other is format (29-second video versus the same text). A pure control is included. The outcome is post-treatment trust with pre-trust covariates. If the effects are due to content, only the science-framing cells should move trust.

power_target.basis: Observed effect of 0.063 with SE about 0.025 at n of about 900. Detecting this at 80% power needs about 1,000 per cell.

briefs.title: Does partisanship moderate the student-video effect?
briefs.question: Do everyday-science videos raise trust more among Republicans than among non-Republicans?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Addresses the missing moderator and the sample. The exploratory interaction of 0.165 in the Science in everyday life arm is untested confirmatory, and partisan effects bear on where the result holds.
briefs.design_sketch: Run the same videos versus control, with sampling quotas on partisanship (about 50% Republican-leaning) and also on a second panel to check the Lucid sample. The interaction between arm and Republican identification is registered as the primary test.
briefs.moderator_or_condition: Republican versus non-Republican identification, and a second sample source beyond Lucid

power_target.basis: Exploratory interaction estimate of 0.165 with SE 0.057 (E2). Interactions need roughly four times the main-effect sample, and the effect is probably inflated, so the target is set for 0.1.

potential.verdict: A follow-up is worth running, but a narrow one. The study's main result is that most messages do nothing detectable. Only the 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video survives multiplicity, and its negative effect (-0.171) is more credible than the gains of about 0.06. Run the replication of the two student videos with a delayed and a behavioural outcome first, because it tests the only consistent positive signal at adequate power. Then run the format-versus-content test and the partisanship moderation test. The literature retrieved is thin, so the debate is only loosely anchored.
